title: Find Peak Element
corePattern: Binary Search on Slope (Peak Finding in Unsorted Array)
interviewTips: Clarify: nums[i] != nums[i+1] for all valid i guarantees a peak exists; any peak index is acceptable, and nums[-1] = nums[n] = -inf for boundary handling.
Trade-off: Linear scan is O(n) and trivially correct, but binary search achieves O(log n) by discarding half based on slope nums[mid] vs nums[mid+1] without needing sorted order.
Edge-case tip: Explicitly discuss n==1, strictly increasing [1,2,3], strictly decreasing [3,2,1], and two-element cases; verify mid+1 never goes out of bounds when loop is left < right.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Linear Scan Brute Force
approaches.intuition: A peak is simply larger than both neighbors, with missing neighbors treated as -infinity. Check every index sequentially and return the first that satisfies the definition.
approaches.theory: By definition nums[-1] = nums[n] = -inf, so at least one peak must exist. Scanning i from 0 to n-1 and comparing nums[i] to left and right neighbors finds it. In worst case we visit all n elements. This is correct but does not exploit the nums[i] != nums[i+1] guarantee for faster search.

timeComplexity.explanation: We visit each element once and do O(1) neighbor comparisons, so time is linear in n.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only a few variables for indices and neighbor values, no extra array.

edgeCases: n==1: [5] returns 0 since both neighbors are -inf
Strictly increasing [1,2,3,4]: peak is last index 3
Strictly decreasing [4,3,2,1]: peak is first index 0

approaches.name: Approach 2: Binary Search on Slope
approaches.intuition: If nums[mid] > nums[mid+1], we are on a descending slope so a peak must be at mid or to the left. Otherwise we are on an ascending slope so a peak must be to the right. Halve the search space each step.
approaches.theory: Because nums[i] != nums[i+1] and boundaries are -inf, the slope test is decisive. Let mid = (left+right)/2. If nums[mid] > nums[mid+1], then interval [left, mid] must contain a peak (either mid is peak if nums[mid] > nums[mid-1], or peak lies left). Else nums[mid] < nums[mid+1], then interval [mid+1, right] must contain a peak. Invariant is maintained while left < right, converging to left==right which is a peak. This is binary search without sorted order, using only local slope.

timeComplexity.explanation: Each iteration halves the search interval [left, right]; at most log2(n) iterations with O(1) work per iteration.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Iterative binary search uses only left, right, mid pointers.

steps: left=0, right=3, mid=1: nums[1]=2 < nums[2]=3 -> ascending, left=2
left=2, right=3, mid=2: nums[2]=3 > nums[3]=1 -> descending, right=2

edgeCases: [1,2,1,3,5,6,4]: binary search may return 1 or 5, both valid peaks
